title: Goodbye.pptx: Why I've Abandoned PowerPoint
author: Joel Kenyon
summary: Joel Kenyon, a science teacher working in a department with highly centralized, well-crafted PowerPoint-based resources, describes how he stopped using slide decks and now teaches exclusively using a visualiser, a pen, and student exercise books. The problem was not centralization itself — which he continues to endorse for workload reduction and consistency — but the way the PPT became the lesson's metronome, imposing its structural logic on when to move, what to cover, and how to adapt, forcing the teacher to serve the slide deck rather than the students. Without slides, his pacing is now governed entirely by reading the room: when students grasp a concept, he moves on regardless of where a hypothetical slide boundary would have fallen; when they struggle, he stays. He identifies deep subject knowledge as the non-negotiable prerequisite — teachers who know their material thoroughly can explain, model, annotate, and improvise without preparation; those who lack it need the slide as a safety net. The shift has also changed his conceptual model of time: from discrete 60-minute lesson units that either finish or don't, to a continuous 20-hour block across which content accumulates, dissolving the guilt of not reaching the slide's end.
points: The PPT becomes a bottleneck when every small pedagogical adaptation — an extra MWB check, a useful conceptual link, a needed scaffold — requires editing a file, making the teacher serve the slide deck rather than the students.

Pacing governed by slide boundaries is inherently student-agnostic; pacing governed by reading the room lets the teacher accelerate with a quick class and extend with a struggling one — a fundamentally different model of time management.

The conceptual shift from 'I have 20 lessons to teach this in' to 'I have 20 hours to teach this' dissolves the guilt of not finishing a lesson and reframes progress as cumulative content coverage across sessions rather than completion of discrete units.

Deep subject knowledge is the non-negotiable prerequisite for abandoning the slide crutch: teachers who know their material can explain, model, and improvise freely; those who lack it need the prepared structure as a safety net.

Centralization and PPT-independence are not mutually exclusive — Kenyon's department still uses centralized Do Now slides, booklet questions, and lesson objectives; what he abandoned was the slide's role as conductor of the lesson, not the coordinated curriculum itself.

If you find yourself more worried about the transition on slide six than the misconception, the learning, or your explanation, it might be time to pick up the pen, turn on your visualiser, and just teach.
quotes: For me, I felt like I, the teacher, wasn’t the most important resource in the room, my PPT was. The pupils get X, but I have a MWB check here or a set of questions there. I might as well do it.
Every individual change I wanted to make to the lesson would resort in my spending time making and editing. All for the sake of having a structure to follow.

The main reason I think this is working is that my pace is now determined, not by my PPT, but instead by the gauging I am getting from pupils. For example, last week I was teaching pressure in solids to my top set Year 8 pupils. They went through that lesson in no time.

Since I started as a teacher, I have been conditioned to think that every lesson is a new lesson. That I have 60 minutes to teach it in and then 60 minutes to teach the next thing. But now, I now see a bunch of content I want the pupils to know, and the number of hours I have to do this in.

The most important part of the teacher’s repertoire is their subject knowledge. The better it is the more they can go deeper into the knowledge, the clearer their explanations, and the easier they will find it to move away from the crutch of a PPT.

If you find yourself more worried about the transition on slide six than the misconception, the learning or your explanation, it might be time to pick up the pen, turn on your visualiser, and just teach.
